# SAME data support experimental detector comparisons

The actual NASA SAME and SAME-R files support a narrow, useful primary task: predict whether the **recorded ISS scatter signal reaches the published 2.0 V alarm reference**, using material and controlled experimental settings. This is a derived experimental response label, not a source-reported alarm event, time-to-alarm estimate, or spacecraft safety judgment. The official combined workbook provides **84 primary material-smoke records: 17 SAME and 67 SAME-R**, with complete controlled inputs and 61 responses at or above 2 V versus 23 below. SAME-R's verified total is **67 heating runs**, not the suggested 66; its 109 records include secondary-aging observations. Reused samples and shared smoke batches require grouped validation. The published saturation of the ISS signal makes threshold classification more defensible than unrestricted analog-response regression, because a saturated signal above the boundary still establishes threshold exceedance. The completed local engineering run uses 81 conservative connected groups and reports grouped nested balanced accuracy **0.8702 ± 0.0764**, compared with **0.5000** for the majority baseline; [metrics.json](metrics.json), [evaluation.md](evaluation.md), and [STATUS.json](../STATUS.json) are authoritative for executed results and current verification status. ([Official combined workbook](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false); [Meyer et al. 2018, section 3.2 and Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/))

## Both investigations are accessible through the PSI API

The audit successfully downloaded the original investigation metadata, experimental CSVs and final reports for PSI-102/SAME and PSI-101/SAME-R, plus the official combined analyzed workbook. Both metadata responses identify investigation version 4 and CC0-1.0. The combined workbook is 4,061,669 bytes with SHA-256 `6d3a539ccf425b1fa8edc19cc75d828f57d650c7ce734d4e7aa686fea9593218`; its file metadata version is 1, distinct from the version 4 used by the investigation download resolver. The resolver with `redirect=false` returns a plain temporary signed URL, which must be fetched separately. That temporary URL is an access mechanism rather than durable provenance and should never be stored in a public manifest. ([SAME metadata](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/repo/investigations/PSI-102); [SAME-R metadata](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/repo/investigations/PSI-101); [Workbook resolver](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false))

The available source modalities are richer than the selected learning table. PSI-102's added-file list contains 104 entries, including legacy XLS run time series, XLSX logs, engineering documents, presentations and videos. PSI-101 includes analyzed spreadsheets, HKP CSV engineering time series, TEM images, videos and reports. Their metadata lists 657,608,178 bytes and 6,308,124,750 bytes respectively; these are inventory totals, **not downloaded byte totals or inspected measurement counts**. The audit did not decode every raw series or image, and cannot establish a total instrument-reading count. The public S3 mirror's root listing contained DSI, OASIS and pk4 rather than SAME data; the working route was the PSI API. ([SAME metadata](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/repo/investigations/PSI-102); [SAME-R metadata](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/repo/investigations/PSI-101); [Public mirror listing](https://nasa-psi.s3.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2&delimiter=/))

The CSVs need different interpretations. SAME's 331-byte experimental table is a planned-condition table with eight numbered Teflon configurations and statements that other materials use the same settings. It is not eight measured independent experiments. SAME-R's 5,674-byte table is an actual run/aging index. The downloaded final reports provide campaign context; the SAME-R report is an 89-page PDF created June 2, 2014. The combined workbook's `Combined Rslts Copy this sheet` worksheet, row 2 headers, is the practical source-reduced table for the baseline pipeline. It avoids applying calibration factors a second time to quantities the experiment authors already corrected. ([SAME CSV](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-102/download?file=PSI-102_Experimental%20table_SAME.csv&version=4&redirect=false); [SAME-R CSV](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Experimental%20table_SAME-R.csv&version=4&redirect=false); [SAME-R report](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final%20Report.pdf&version=4&redirect=false))

## Eighty-four primary records require conservative sample grouping

The combined worksheet has **154 recognized flight records: 45 SAME and 109 SAME-R**. SAME's 45 records contain 29 numeric heating identifiers, including 20 DBP calibration records across 12 heating identifiers. Excluding DBP leaves 25 material-smoke records across 17 primary heating runs. SAME-R has 67 primary heating identifiers and 42 secondary suffix-`a` records. The SAME-R final report's Flight Operation section, PDF page 3, independently reports 67 runs including two using reused samples, and 109 entries when secondary aging is listed separately. ([Workbook](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false); [SAME-R final report](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final%20Report.pdf&version=4&redirect=false))

| Independence level | SAME material-smoke subset | SAME-R | Permitted interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Campaigns | 1 | 1 | Two domains; campaign-shift stress testing, not a population of hardware designs |
| Primary heating runs | 17 | 67 | Primary learning records before reuse grouping |
| Primary physical sample groups | 17 carousel/position pairs | 65 sample IDs | Conservative reuse grouping; 82 primary groups before any extra conservative links |
| Primary plus secondary records | 25 | 109 | Repeated observations; cannot be split independently |
| All-row connected run/sample components | 17 material-smoke units unless source IDs add links | 64 | Conservative full-observation grouping includes an ambiguous secondary identity |
| Raw time-series readings | Not enumerated | Not enumerated | No claim of reading-level sample size |

SAME-R sample L14 is reused in runs 54 and 57; the latter is explicitly described as a reburn. K08 is reused in runs 85 and 90. The secondary record 51a lists K02 even though its parent 51 lists K01, while 61/61a also list K02. The audit cannot correct that identity with confidence. Grouping the full table by connected components sharing either a numeric run or a sample ID conservatively links that ambiguity; a primary-only grouping can retain the 82 verified primary physical-sample units. These alternatives differ in effective group count, so the executed preprocessing and metrics must state which was used. ([Workbook](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false))

A positive heating-duration cell is insufficient to identify primary runs. SAME 29a, 41a, 46a and 47a retain positive heating durations, as does SAME-R 51a. The primary model should explicitly exclude secondary suffix-`a` identifiers and retain those rows for descriptive aging displays. SAME's fan-problem and flat-profile flags are `n`; SAME-R's cells are blank, which means unknown rather than verified absence. These choices reduce ambiguity without inventing heating settings for follow-up observations. ([Workbook](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false))

## Common controls support an ISS response label, with explicit calibration limits

Material, heating, airflow and aging are experimentally controlled. The 2018 paper describes software control of these settings, and the combined workbook provides complete N/O/P/Q/R inputs for all 84 primary rows. SAME-R's report warns that the same resistance-ratio setpoint can produce different actual sample temperatures. Rt/R0 is therefore a legitimate input available before a run, but an imperfect physical surrogate for sample temperature. The source-derived temperature column CE should not be silently substituted as a pre-experiment control. Net aging U is not identical to programmed primary aging Q and should remain separately named. ([Meyer et al. 2018, section 2.2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/); [Workbook](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false); [SAME-R report, PDF pp2–3](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final%20Report.pdf&version=4&redirect=false))

| Source column | Variable and unit | Role and provenance | Cross-campaign treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | Material | Controlled category; `source_reported` | Kapton, Lampwick, Silicone, Teflon; Pyrell only in SAME-R; DBP excluded |
| N | Inlet velocity, cm/s | Controlled; `source_reported` | Identity units; SAME 2–8, SAME-R 0–8.1 |
| O | Rt/R0, dimensionless | Controlled heating setpoint; `source_reported` | Identity; SAME 1.245–1.48, SAME-R 1.22–1.48 |
| P | Heating duration, s | Controlled; `source_reported` | Primary rows only; SAME 10–60, SAME-R 60–120 |
| Q | Primary aging duration, s | Controlled; `source_reported` | Identity; SAME 8–720, SAME-R 1–720 |
| R | Primary mixing duration, s | Controlled; `source_reported` | Identity; SAME 0–8, SAME-R 8 |
| U | Net aging duration, s | Source timing-derived quantity | Separate descriptive field, not an interchangeable control |
| AW | ISS scatter, V | Measured analog output; `source_reported` | Author-combined voltage channel; use for threshold labeling only |
| AW >= 2.0 V | Recorded alarm-level exceedance | Deterministic `derived` label | Published Figure 9 boundary; not source-reported alarm event |
| AX / AY | STS response / offset, V | Measured channels and background | Not harmonized for modeling; operation flags and offset convention required |
| BL / BM | M0, number/cm³; M1, mm/cm³ | Source-reduced moments | Preserve source calibration; not condition-model inputs |
| BQ | Corrected DustTrak mass, mg/m³ | Source-reduced measured quantity | Material-specific calibration already applied; no double correction |
| BR | Count mean diameter, μm | Source-reported deterministic derivation | Check against 1000 M1/M0; no lognormal assumption |
| BS / BU / BV | Mass-equivalent diameter / geometric spread / geometric diameter | Source-derived quantities | Additional density, shape or lognormal assumptions require explicit labels |
| BN / BO | MPASS quantities | SAME-R-specific | Not instrument-equivalent with SAME |
| CB / CC / CD / CE | Calibration, dilution, density, derived temperature | Source analysis state | Preserve provenance; not universally interchangeable controls |

This map deliberately chooses an author-reduced common channel instead of claiming that every raw instrument is calibrated identically. The nominal P-Trak range is 0–100,000 particles/cm³ with a nominal 20 nm–1 μm size range, while DustTrak's documented range is 0.001–100 mg/m³; dilution and material calibration alter how these ranges relate to source-reduced concentrations. They must not be used as universal censoring thresholds on corrected workbook values. Exact per-record ISS saturation state, electronic resolution, background uncertainty and raw-channel limit of detection were not independently reconstructed. The approximately 6.25 V plateau is consistent with published saturation, but no precise invented cutoff should replace the source voltage. Preserve the reported value and mark saturation as unresolved at the individual-row level; restrict its use to the still-identifiable threshold label. ([Properties of Smoke from Overheated Materials in Low-Gravity, PDF pp4–5](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20120012884/downloads/20120012884.pdf); [Meyer et al. 2018, section 3.2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/))

ISS AW is numeric in every recognized flight row. Applying the verified 2 V boundary gives SAME 13 positive and 4 negative primary labels, and SAME-R 48 positive and 19 negative. Shuttle data cannot be labeled by interpreting zero as no detection: the source includes not-used flags and zero signals, as well as near-negative-zero readings. The 2018 paper plots Shuttle baseline-to-response differences after acquisition scaling and reports fewer Shuttle measurements because its 3 L/min pump prevents aging experiments. It does not justify an exact Shuttle alarm threshold inferred from a graph. Missing, below-detection-limit, saturation and genuine numeric zero must stay distinct. No human annotations were created; deterministic threshold labels have provenance `derived`. ([Workbook](https://psi.nasa.gov/geode-py/ws/studies/PSI-101/download?file=PSI-101_Analyzed%20Data_SAME%2C%20SAME-R_Results.xlsx&version=4&redirect=false); [Meyer et al. 2018, Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/))

## Threshold classification offers the clearest defensible dashboard feature

The task-selection scores below are **agent-annotated engineering judgments on a 1–5 scale**, where 5 is strongest; they are not measured model performance or a scientific risk score. The eight columns correspond to the requested evidence criteria. Leakage scores reward lower risk. Independent-unit scores reflect the small, grouped sample rather than the much larger raw reading inventory.

| Candidate task | Scientific relevance | Dashboard utility | Independent units | Label quality | Inputs at inference | Leakage/generalization | Compute feasibility | Honest validation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **ISS >=2 V from controlled conditions** | **5** | **5** | **3** | **4** | **5** | **3** | **5** | **4** |
| ISS analog voltage from conditions | 5 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 5 | 3 |
| Particle-size statistics from conditions | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 5 | 4 |
| Material identification from measured signatures | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 4 |
| Descriptive detector-coverage gaps | 5 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 5 | 3 |

Threshold classification answers a concrete dashboard question: “For a tested material and these controlled settings, did comparable experiment smoke reach the ISS detector's recorded alarm level?” It uses material plus airflow, resistance ratio, heating duration, programmed primary aging and mixing. Outputs should include the predicted class, `value_kind=predicted`, version, applicable training domain and an empirical same-material condition-distance OOD flag. Display the measured scatter and derived reference separately from predictions. Unseen materials must be rejected; accepted sparse combinations should be flagged, and numeric inputs outside the observed ranges must raise an error or explicit warning. A precomputed table can render observed tests without a model call. Its measured or derived reference is evidence; predictions fitted to those same rows are illustrations unless clearly replaced by held-out predictions.

Analog regression loses information at the saturation ceiling and would require a credible censoring model. Particle-size prediction remains a feasible alternative but answers a less direct detector question and inherits instrument/density/morphology assumptions. Predicting M1/M0 from M1 and M0 would be algebraic leakage, not learning. Material identification requires measured signatures at inference and serves a different diagnostic use case. Descriptive gap analysis is valuable as a companion view, but cannot turn gaps in a sparse test matrix into claims of real spacecraft danger. These are task-selection decisions, not empirical rankings among trained model families. ([Meyer et al. 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/); [Particle Morphology and Size Results, equations and calibration discussion](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20130000422/downloads/20130000422.pdf))

The model-family comparison must start with a majority baseline and a simple classifier. Grouped nested validation should select among candidates inside training folds and reserve outer folds for the headline estimate. Repeated samples remain together; campaign transfer is reported separately on supported materials, because SAME has no Pyrell examples. Per-material metrics must state when a material has only one observed class, making balanced accuracy or PR-AUC uninformative. No uncertainty intervals are justified by this audit alone. The selected scope is **these tested materials, source-reduced experiments and condition ranges**, not untested fuels, flaming combustion, detector timing, full-scale transport or operational fire certification.

## Published values can check derivations without becoming new ground truth

The reference audit visually checked Figure 9's ISS alarm boundary against its 2.0 V axis tick. It also extracted and visually verified every row of NTRS 20130000422 Table 1, PDF page 7, saving a rendered image in `data/references/20130000422_table1.png`. The following values are source-reported calculations in μm, not newly measured examples. They permit formula and rounding checks, and can support a direct workbook comparison only after the baseline configuration and aggregation have been matched. No such per-run matching is claimed in this report. ([2018 Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/); [2012 Table 1](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20130000422/downloads/20130000422.pdf))

| Material | Count mean unaged / aged 720 s, μm | Diameter of average mass unaged / aged 720 s, μm |
|---|---|---|
| Kapton | 0.056 / 0.109 | 0.101 / 0.161 |
| Lampwick | 0.128 / 0.276 | 0.258 / 0.398 |
| Silicone | 0.196 / 0.355 | 0.465 / 0.619 |
| Teflon | 0.101 / 0.105 | 0.170 / 0.232 |
| Pyrell | 0.204 / 0.359 | 0.384 / 0.539 |

Count mean diameter is M1/M0 and diameter of average mass is (M3/M0)^(1/3). Neither moment ratio alone requires lognormality. Converting mass into a third moment requires particle-density and spherical-equivalent interpretation; obtaining geometric mean diameter and geometric standard deviation adds a lognormal assumption. For a lognormal distribution, count mean is Dg exp(0.5 ln²σg), and diameter of average mass is Dg exp(1.5 ln²σg). Formula agreement with the rounded table is a consistency check, not external predictive validation. The 2015 moment-method paper reports stronger support for near-spherical/lognormal assumptions for Kapton and lampwick, while aggregate morphology and silicone instability constrain other materials. ([2012 equations (2), (6), (7)](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20130000422/downloads/20130000422.pdf); [Meyer et al. 2015](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02786826.2015.1025124))

**The unaged Teflon row fails this internal formula check and remains an unresolved source-table inconsistency.** A second visual inspection confirms that the source prints geometric diameter 0.081 μm, geometric standard deviation 2.198, count mean 0.101 μm and average-mass diameter 0.170 μm. Applying the printed lognormal identities to the geometric pair instead yields **0.110450 μm** and **0.205367 μm**. Rounding bounds do not bridge either discrepancy: allowing ±0.0005 on the printed geometric parameters yields count mean 0.109749–0.111152 μm and average-mass diameter 0.203989–0.206745 μm. The publication does not document independent column averaging or explain this row. Averaging, a typographical error, or another processing difference would be speculative explanations. The original values remain unchanged, and this row must be excluded from any assertion of passed formula agreement. Executed calculations are preserved in `data/references/teflon_table1_check.json` and [external_checks.csv](external_checks.csv). This discrepancy does not alter the separate ISS-threshold labels. ([Original Table 1, PDF p7](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20130000422/downloads/20130000422.pdf))

Several supplied bibliographic descriptions need correction. NTRS 20120012884 is titled *Properties of Smoke from Overheated Materials in Low-Gravity*. The NIST link identifies a March 5, 2010 *Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)* Final Report led by David L. Urban and colleagues; a Yang-led NASA TM was not verified. No separate NASA 2021 report was located. The 2018 detector manuscript became available in PMC on March 1, 2021, a plausible source of the date confusion but not proof of the intended reference. The challenge URL returned a fetch error, so its content was not independently verified. These gaps should remain explicit rather than be filled with assumed citations. ([NTRS paper](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20120012884/downloads/20120012884.pdf); [NIST final report](https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=904707); [2018 manuscript metadata](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/))

The research audit and reference extraction are `TESTED_LOCALLY`. Training and nested evaluation completed on both local CPU and standard CPU Colab with 84 primary records and 81 conservative connected groups. The finalized notebook passed all **36 tests in Colab**, and its downloaded export passed all **36 tests locally**. The headline balanced accuracy is 0.8701515 ± 0.0763605 versus the majority baseline's 0.5; local and Colab fold scores agree exactly. The Colab runtime was stopped after retrieval. [evaluation.md](evaluation.md), [metrics.json](metrics.json), [external_checks.csv](external_checks.csv), [out_of_fold_predictions.csv](out_of_fold_predictions.csv) and [STATUS.json](../STATUS.json) contain the executed engineering results and current per-deliverable status, including storage verification.

The dashboard can place detector-response evidence beside model_a's flame-spread regression and model_b's video-derived flame progression, while preserving their distinct experiments and units. The useful connection is a comparison of experimental capabilities—spread, observed flame behavior and recorded smoke-detector response—without implying that the three datasets form synchronized measurements of one fire.
